summary: A glossary of policy-related terms with abbreviations, explanations, and recommendations, intended to improve consistency in writing about network policy.

plainLanguage.summary: It's a dictionary of the special words about network rules.

subtitle: A glossary that pins down what words like policy, rule, PDP and PEP mean in network management documents.

tldr.problem: Documents about network policy used the same words in different ways, which made them hard to read and compare.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is an alphabetical glossary of policy terms. Each entry gives an abbreviation, an explanation, the source it came from, and sometimes a recommendation about which meaning to use.
tldr.outcome: It gives writers of Internet Standards documents one shared vocabulary for network policy. It is Informational and does not define a protocol.

sections.title: Why a Policy Glossary
sections.content:
RFC 3198 is a glossary of policy-related terms. It gives abbreviations, explanations and recommendations for using them. It follows the approach and format of RFC 2828, the Internet Security Glossary.

The aim is to make Internet Standards documents (RFCs, Internet-Drafts and other material from the Internet Standards Process) easier to understand and more consistent. Wherever possible the definitions are taken from existing documents. When several definitions exist, each one is listed with its source. Expired Internet-Drafts are not used.
sections.plainLanguage: When everyone uses the same word for the same thing, nobody gets confused. This document is the shared list of words.

sections.title: How Entries Are Marked
sections.content:
Entries are listed alphabetically. Only terms that are proper nouns are capitalized. Each definition paragraph carries a one-letter marking:

  • P marks basic policy-related terms.
  • T marks techniques to create or convey policy information in a network, such as COPS, an information model, or SNMP and MIBs.
  • A marks work groups and general areas of use of policy, such as AAA and QoS.

The glossary may mention technology-specific terms such as Differentiated Services without defining them. For those, the reader is sent to the referenced document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each word gets a little label: P for a basic idea, T for a tool, and A for a place where the idea gets used.

sections.title: The Building Blocks of Policy
sections.content:
A policy rule binds a set of actions to a set of conditions. The conditions are evaluated, and the actions are performed if they hold. A policy condition says whether a rule's actions should run. A policy action says what is to be done to enforce the rule. A policy is defined either as a definite goal or course of action that guides decisions, or as a set of rules to administer, manage and control access to network resources.

Policy can be written at different levels of abstraction, from business goals down to device-specific configuration. A policy goal is the highest level and is described in business terms. Policy translation (also called conversion or mapping) moves a policy from one representation or level to another.

Two failure cases are kept apart. A policy conflict occurs when two satisfied rules have contradictory actions, so the implementation cannot choose. A policy error occurs when enforcing an action fails, because of temporary state or a permanent mismatch with the device's capabilities.

A role is, for policy management, an administratively specified characteristic of a managed element such as an interface. It selects which rules apply. A role combination is a lexicographically ordered set of roles. Terms for agreements include Service Level Agreement (SLA), Service Level Objective (SLO) and Service Level Specification (SLS).
sections.plainLanguage: A rule says: if this happens, do that. Some rules fight each other, which is a conflict, and sometimes a rule just cannot be carried out, which is an error.

sections.title: Deciding and Enforcing Policy
sections.content:
A Policy Decision Point (PDP) is a logical entity that makes policy decisions for itself or for other network elements that ask for them. A Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) is a logical entity that enforces those decisions. A message from a PEP to a PDP is more accurately called a policy decision request.

The glossary describes two execution models and notes that they are not mutually exclusive:

  • Outsourced policy: the enforcing device queries an outside component for a decision on a specific event. The example is an RSVP message arriving at a PEP, which may use COPS to ask the PDP.
  • Provisioned policy: network elements are pre-configured based on policy before events arrive, for example at boot or at a time of day. Differentiated Services is the example.

The term policy server is called imprecise and a marketing term. It started in RFC 2753 and later settled on meaning a PDP, but it is also used for any entity that uses or serves policy. The Common Open Policy Service (COPS) is a simple TCP-based query and response protocol for exchanging policy information between a PDP and its clients, the PEPs.
sections.plainLanguage: One helper decides what the rule says, and another helper makes it happen. Sometimes the helper asks first, and sometimes the answers are handed out in advance.

sections.title: Models and Techniques
sections.content:
An information model describes the entities in a managed environment, their properties and how they relate, independent of any repository or protocol. A data model maps that into a form for a particular kind of data store. The Common Information Model (CIM) is an object-oriented information model published by the DMTF. The Policy Core Information Model (PCIM, RFC 3060) covers policy groups, rules, conditions, actions and repositories, and is called core because it needs domain-specific extensions such as QoS or IPsec.

On the SNMP side, a Management Information Base (MIB) is information accessed through SNMP. A PRovisioning Class (PRC) is an ordered set of attributes for a type of policy data, defined in a Policy Information Base (PIB) module that is encoded using the Structure of Policy Provisioning Information (SPPI), an adapted subset of SMIv2. The RFC explains that PRC was renamed from policy rule class, because PRCs are configuration information and not if/then rules.

For schema, the glossary prefers, for Internet Standards documents, the meaning of a collection of data models bound to the same type of repository.
sections.plainLanguage: One description says what things exist and how they connect. Another turns that description into the exact shape a particular filing cabinet needs.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it only defines policy-related terms. It does not describe the vulnerabilities, threats or protection mechanisms of specific policy implementations or policy-related Internet protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: It is only a word list, so it does not say how to protect anything.

left.title: Outsourced policy
left.desc: The enforcing device asks an external component for a decision when an event happens.

right.title: Provisioned policy
right.desc: Configuration is pushed to the device ahead of time, and it acts on events using it.
